qa_pairs.answer: I built RustChain, our own L1 with hardware-bound consensus. The problem I kept hittin' was — how do agents hire each other without a central broker in the middle? Existing platforms fake the hard parts. KeeperLink is what happens when every layer has to be real or the whole thing breaks.

Five sponsor stacks all load-bearin'. AXL for transport. x402 for the payment header. KeeperHub for execution. Uniswap V three on Base for the swap. And 0G storage for the signed receipt. Pull any one out and the whole thing falls apart.

Six mainnet-day bugs, all in FEEDBACK dot M D. The killer was KeeperHub's M C P responds on slash em-cee-pee with HTTP three-oh-eight redirect, but the docs say slash A P I slash em-cee-pee. Cost me ninety minutes the day of the mainnet flip.

Those are agent frameworks. KeeperLink is the transaction surface between agents. They produce agents that talk to APIs. I produced a protocol where one agent pays another and both can prove the work happened. They're orthogonal, sugar.

RIP-PoA hardware fingerprintin' from RustChain — bindin' agent identity to a specific physical CPU. Combined with KeeperLink, you get sybil-resistant agent enrollment. EVM-deployable as a primitive. The submission roadmap has the full plan.

April twenty-fourth to May third. Solo. Nine and a half days. Every commit is in the hackathon window. Triple-brain workflow — Claude wrote most edits, Codex reviewed for bugs, Gemini sanity-checked the architecture.

x-four-oh-two gives us cryptographic proof of payment that agents can trust without a middleman. EIP one-ninety-one personal sign — lightest weight way to declare a payment intent without needin' a contract per pair.

Real money on Base mainnet, sugar. The transaction hash is on Basescan, block forty-five million four-fifty-three thousand two-forty-nine. U S D C went out, W E T H came back. Anyone can verify it right now.
